dialog.body: Zoning and Inspections, this is Anita. How can I help you?

Hello, hello! Great, wonderful, I got the right office, I hope. My name is Tito Pina, and I'm calling for my mother. She's in her eighties, and she wants a fence in the yard. A fence company gave us a quote, and before we sign anything I want to check with you people first.
Good thinking, checking first. Where's the property, Mr. Pina?
167 Gidley Street. That's the Fifth Ward, yes. Her house, not mine. I live across town.
Okay, 167 Gidley. And what kind of fence are we talking about?

Chain-link! Four feet tall. Nothing fancy, wonderful and simple. The man said four feet is a nice standard height. So my question is, what are the rules on fences here? Is there paperwork? Do we need a permit, or is it just, you put it up and that's that?

Generally, yes, a fence usually needs a permit in Newport, even a lower one. But the details depend on the property, like where the lot lines are and how close to the street it sits. Do you know if it's going along the front, or around the back?

Hmm. Around the back, I think, and a little down the side. Or maybe the front also? The quote says, uh, one hundred and, I don't have it in front of me. Wait, I do. It says a hundred and twenty linear feet. Is that the word? Linear?
Yes, linear feet is just the total length. So a hundred and twenty feet. Does the quote say anything about the front yard, or does it just say rear and side?

Rear and side. Okay, wonderful. But, now I'm confused, you said a permit, but the fence man said the company takes care of everything. Does that mean he gets the permit? Or no permit? I didn't understand that part.

Some companies do pull the permit for you, and some leave it to the homeowner. I'd ask him directly, and ask him to put it in writing on the quote. Either way, the permit is for the property, so your mother's name would be on the application.
Her name, okay. Great. But she's not, you know, she doesn't go out much. Can I do it for her?
The contractor or a family member can usually submit it for the owner. We'd want her to sign off on it, though. Let me ask, is she the owner on the deed, or is the house in somebody else's name?
Hers. Hers, I'm sure. My father put it in both names, and then, well, it's hers now. I think. Should I check?

It'd be good to be sure. The assessor's office could confirm who's on record. Now, a permit application will ask for a sketch showing where the fence goes. A simple drawing of the lot with the fence line is fine.
A drawing! I can't draw, but my niece... no, wait, the fence man can draw it, right? Wonderful. Okay. And the fee? How much is the fee for this? I want to know before I sign the quote.

I can't quote you an exact number off the top of my head, and it can depend on the project value. The fee schedule is posted, and I can have someone call you back with the amount for a fence that size. Would that work?
Yes, great! Call me at 401-555-0197. That's the landline, so if I don't answer, I'm out, I have a union meeting I'm headed to right after this, so you'll catch me later or leave a message.
Got it, 401-555-0197, for Tito Pina, about a four-foot chain-link fence at 167 Gidley. I'll also note that you want to know if the fence company handles the permit.
Yes, yes, that's it exactly. And so, to be clear, I do not sign until I hear from you. Right? Or is it okay to sign, if the permit comes after?
I'd hold off until you know who's pulling the permit and what it costs. Nothing says you can't sign, but you'll want it clear in the contract.
Okay, okay. Hold off. Wonderful. Thank you, Anita, is that right, Anita? You've been so helpful!
Yes, Anita. You're welcome, Mr. Pina. Someone will call you back. Enjoy your meeting.
Great, thank you! Goodbye!
